messages.author: 693eee7c90ae0495
messages.subject: VCP, high densities, snapshot
parts:
Hi Distance-samplers,
I have been using VCP counts to assess songbird densities in German
forested areas as described by BIBBY et al. 1992 (two bands, 0-30 m and
30 m - infinity; counting period 6 and 10 min., resp.). The resulting
densities were far to high (factor 3 or so compared to expected densities
from 'normal' territory mapping results in literature), as already
experienced by BIBBY et al. 1985.
BIBBY et al. 2000 and BUCKLAND et al. 2001 address the problem of high
densities and advocate for snapshot techniques and the use of precise
distance measurements for each individual recorded. As I only found
general hints on this topic in both works, I would very much like to know
about quantitative considerations on errors comparing e.g. 10 min. full
count vs. snapshot and two counting bands vs. precise distance. Can
missing snapshots/precise distances be considered a satisfying explanation
for those high densities ?
Any comments or hints on citable references will be highly appreciated.
Greetings,
Wilken


References:

BIBBY, C.J., BURGESS, N.D. & HILL, D.A. 1992. Bird Census Techniques.
Academic Press, London.

BIBBY, C.J., BURGESS, N.D., HILL, D.A., MUSTOE, S.H. 2000. Bird Census
Techniques. 2nd Ed. Academic Press, London.

BIBBY, C.J., PHILLIPS, B.N. & SEDDON, A.J. 1985. Birds of restocked
conifer plantations in Wales. Journal of Applied Ecology 22: 619-633.

BUCKLAND, S.T., ANDERSON, D.R., BURNHAM, K.P., LAAKE, J.L., BORCHERS, D.L.
& THOMAS, L. 2001. Introduction into Distance Sampling. Oxford University
Press, Oxf.

messages.author: a2f0d511c0c864c7
messages.subject: Re: VCP, high densities, snapshot
parts:
Hi Wilken and group,

Of general interest perhaps is a newly published paper by T. R. Shankar Raman
comparing bird counting techniques in a (tropical) forest. It's in the January
issue of Ibis (2003) vol. 145: pp. 9-21.

He concluded that 'inflated' density estimates from VCPM were a product of
bird movement during the count period. While such movement should be a
problem, especially in 10 minute counts, I'm not sure the above paper
quantifies the overall effect very accurately - there may even be greater
errors (underestimation) in the territory mapping (which he uses as the
baseline of 'true' density) than there are in the distance sampling methods.

I have seen almost nothing in the literature on the quest for compromise point
count periods that minimise bias due to bird movement, while at the same time
maintaining detection probability over crucial distances. Optimum count
periods should vary between bird groups and between habitats. Maybe someone on
the list knows of work on this?


Dr Stuart J. Marsden
Senior Lecturer in Biogeography and Conservation Biology

messages.author: c7ef6a5cf6945b0b
messages.subject: VCP, high densities, snapshot
parts:
Hello All,

Yes, I agree with Stuart that optimal counting periods for point-transects
do vary per species. During a study I was conducting in New Zealand
temperate rain forest, I believed that a five-minute counting period was
overestimating abundances for honeyeaters, and started experimenting with
snapshot counts. These snapshot counts were executed after a three minute
waiting and observing period - they consistently yielded lower estimates
of density for my faster moving species.

In contrast I found that this snapshot technique was woefully inadequate
for species such as our large endemic wood pigeon - for which even up to a
ten minute period was more suitable due to their frequently silent and
still presence in the canopy. These pigeons are also generally extremely
noisy when entering, leaving, or moving within the point transect area and
therefore over-estimations of density due to undetected movement during
the long count were not a problem.

I'm currently whipping a paper into shape and hope to submit these results
for publication in the near future.

In fact the importance of taking the time to determine how best to apply
distance techniques on a species specific basis can not be overemphasized:
Another paper (on which I was just a co-author) that has ben submitted to
Ibis, showed line-transects to perform extremely well on a NZ passerine
of known population size. Whereas, both one-minute and five-minute
point-transects vastly overestimated population estimates. -- However,
these point-transect counts were conducted after a five-minute standing,
waiting, period and I believe that this slightly curious species may have
been inclined to move towards a standing observer - and subsequently,
that these over inflated point-transect results may be an example of the
dramatic effect that movement towards the observer can have on estimates
of density. I am following up on this and will be trying to establish
whether or not these birds do indeed react in this way to a standing
observer.

Cheers, Rosemary
